topics.label: Deductions
topics.period: Check eligibility and record requirements for the income year of the expense.

topics.label: Starting a business
topics.period: Use the entity, activity and income year being assessed.

topics.label: GST and BAS
topics.period: Use the BAS period, GST accounting basis and account due date being reviewed.

topics.label: Payroll and super
topics.period: Use the pay date and applicable payroll rules. Super questions distinguish the regime from July 2026.

topics.label: Bookkeeping and close

questions.question: What will my income tax bill be?
questions.answer: Start with taxable income for the correct income year, then account for levies, offsets, study loans and tax already withheld. A basic tax bracket result alone is incomplete.
steps: Gather income statements, investment statements, deductible expenses and PAYG credits.
Use the ATO return estimate and reconcile each adjustment before treating it as a budget.
questions.boundary: The linked experimental income tax worksheet excludes levies and offsets; check its supported years.
questions.fact: For 2026-27, a resident pays no tax on the first $18,200, 15% from $18,201 to $45,000, 30% to $135,000, 37% to $190,000 and 45% above that, plus the 2% Medicare levy.

questions.question: Which expenses reduce my taxable income?
questions.answer: An expense needs a connection to assessable income and the evidence required for that type of claim. Private spending and reimbursed amounts need separate treatment.
steps: List each expense, its purpose, date, amount and reimbursement.
Record your work use calculation and check the ATO category before claiming.
questions.boundary: A receipt proves spending, but does not by itself establish deductibility.
questions.fact: To claim a work-related expense, you must have paid it yourself without reimbursement, it must directly relate to earning your income, and you need a record to prove it, usually a receipt. From 2026-27, eligible taxpayers can claim a standard deduction of up to $1,000 for work-related expenses without records; it is reduced by any work-related expenses they claim that it covers.

questions.question: What steps are involved in completing a return?
questions.answer: Collect the year’s records, reconcile them with pre-fill information, calculate supported claims, then review and lodge through an authorised channel.
steps: Check income statements are ready and account for income missing from pre-fill.
Keep a copy of the reviewed return, declaration and lodgement receipt.
questions.boundary: The checklist prepares your records; lodgement happens with the ATO or your registered agent.
questions.fact: Most pre-fill data from employers, banks, health funds and government agencies is finalised by the end of July; check that it includes all your income before you lodge. If you lodge your own return, it is due by 31 October; to use a registered tax agent’s later dates, engage them before then.

questions.question: Where can I obtain or recover my TFN?
questions.answer: Use the ATO’s TFN application or lost-TFN route. The right application process depends on residency and circumstances.
steps: If you already have a TFN, use the ATO recovery instructions before applying again.
Complete any identity checks directly with the official service.
questions.boundary: Do not put a TFN or identity documents into this website or a public issue.
questions.fact: Applying for a TFN is free, online or on paper depending on your residency and circumstances. If you have a TFN but can’t remember it, find it in ATO online services through myGov, or phone the ATO.

questions.question: What dates govern the annual tax cycle?
questions.answer: Build a calendar from the dates that apply to your return, activity statements, payroll and entity obligations.
steps: Record the period, lodgement date, payment date and responsible person for each obligation.
Confirm the dates in your ATO account or with your registered agent; record any approved extension.
questions.boundary: An agent’s program or a particular account can have different dates from a general calendar.
questions.fact: The income year runs from 1 July to 30 June. A return you lodge yourself is due by 31 October, quarterly BAS is due on 28 October, 28 February, 28 April and 28 July, and STP finalisation is due by 14 July.

questions.question: Which methods can I use to settle my tax bill?
questions.answer: Use the ATO payment instructions for the relevant account and payment reference.
steps: Check the amount owing and available payment methods in the official service.
Allow for processing time and keep the receipt; reconcile the payment when it appears.
questions.boundary: This website does not collect payments or supply bank details.
questions.fact: You can pay the ATO by BPAY, direct deposit, debit or credit card, Government EasyPay, in person at Australia Post or through an international money remitter.

questions.question: Which earnings are taxable?
questions.answer: Check each source of income against the ATO’s categories. Amounts missing from pre-fill still need review.
steps: Reconcile employment, business, investment, government and foreign income records.
List unusual receipts separately and record why they are included or excluded.
questions.boundary: A bank deposit is not automatically taxable income, and taxable income is not limited to deposits.
questions.fact: You must declare employment income, government payments and allowances, investment income such as interest, dividends, rent and capital gains, business, partnership and trust income, super pensions and annuities, and foreign income. Some compensation and insurance payments, scholarships, prizes and awards are also taxable.

questions.question: How long will the tax return process take?
questions.answer: Separate your preparation time from the ATO’s processing time. Missing records, amendments and reviews can extend the overall process.
steps: Complete the record checklist before setting a preparation deadline.
After lodgement, use the official progress service and respond to any information request.
questions.boundary: No refund date or processing outcome is guaranteed here.
questions.fact: Most returns lodged online are processed within 12 business days. For a paper return, most refunds are issued within 50 business days.

questions.question: Where can I submit a completed return?
questions.answer: Individuals can use the lodgement options on the ATO’s tax return page, including myTax where eligible, a registered agent or paper.
steps: Choose the route for your circumstances and confirm the income year.
Review the declaration and save the lodgement receipt after submission.
questions.boundary: The site supplies preparation guidance and does not submit returns.
questions.fact: You can lodge online with myTax, through a registered tax agent or on paper by mail. Registered tax agents are the only people who can charge a fee to prepare and lodge your return.

questions.question: Which tax rules changed from 1 July 2026?
questions.answer: Most changes start on 1 July, so compare 2025-26 with 2026-27 rather than calendar years.
steps: Use the ATO 'Before you prepare your tax return' guidance for each year.
Record each changed rate or rule, effective date, source and affected calculation in a change log.
questions.boundary: An announcement is not evidence that a measure applied to your transaction. This is a review procedure, not an exhaustive legislative history.
questions.fact: From 1 July 2026, the 16% personal tax rate fell to 15%, Payday Super generally requires contributions to reach the fund within 7 business days of payday, the $20,000 instant asset write-off became permanent for small businesses and the cents per kilometre rate rose to 91 cents.

questions.question: How do I calculate my working-from-home deduction?
questions.answer: Compare the eligible working-from-home methods for the income year using the required evidence for each.
steps: Record actual hours worked at home and the costs or rate that the chosen method covers.
Keep separately claimed costs out of any category already included in the chosen method.
questions.boundary: Eligibility, rates and record requirements must be checked for the year; this site does not select the method for you.
questions.fact: Under the fixed rate method, you claim 70 cents for each hour you work from home in 2024-25 and 2025-26. The actual cost method is the alternative.

questions.question: What records do I need to support my working-from-home claim?
questions.answer: Keep evidence of hours and costs that supports the particular working-from-home method you use.
steps: Record dates and hours throughout the required period and retain bills or receipts.
Keep a note of the method, year, work use basis and costs excluded to prevent double claims.
questions.boundary: A reconstructed estimate may not meet the ATO’s requirements for your method.
questions.fact: For the fixed rate method, keep a record of the actual hours you work from home for the whole year, such as a timesheet, roster or diary, because estimates are not accepted. Also keep at least one record, such as a bill, for each running expense the rate covers.

questions.question: Should I use the cents-per-kilometre or logbook method for car expenses?
questions.answer: Compare the methods you are eligible to use, using the same car and income year.
steps: For cents per kilometre, document eligible kilometres and check the year’s rate and cap.
For the logbook method, gather a valid logbook, odometer readings and actual running costs.
questions.boundary: Vehicle type, ownership and entity structure can change which methods are available.
questions.fact: The cents per kilometre rate is 91 cents for 2026-27 (88 cents for 2024-25 and 2025-26), capped at 5,000 business kilometres per car. The logbook method has no kilometre cap but needs a valid logbook.

questions.question: How do I keep a valid vehicle logbook?
questions.answer: A useful logbook records each business trip and lets another person check the business use percentage.
steps: Record the required trip dates, odometer readings, distance and business purpose.
Keep opening and closing odometer readings and review whether changed use requires a new logbook.
questions.boundary: Check the ATO’s required recording period and validity conditions before relying on the logbook.
questions.fact: A logbook must cover at least 12 continuous weeks and be broadly representative of your travel. It stays valid for 5 years, but you need a new 12-week logbook if your circumstances change.

questions.question: How do I calculate the work-related share of phone and internet expenses?
questions.answer: Apply a supported work use percentage to eligible phone and internet costs.
steps: Gather bills and a representative usage record that distinguishes private from work use.
Use the business use calculator and retain the usage calculation with the result.
questions.boundary: Do not separately claim costs already covered by your chosen working-from-home method.
questions.fact: Work out your work use percentage on a reasonable basis over a continuous 4-week period, using an itemised bill or your own record of work and private calls and internet use, then apply it to the whole income year.

questions.question: Can I deduct a laptop or tools immediately, or must I depreciate them?
questions.answer: Separate employee deductions from business asset rules, then identify whether immediate deduction or decline in value applies.
steps: Record cost, acquisition date, first use, work use share and whether the item forms part of a set.
Check the applicable year’s asset rules and retain the calculation in an asset register.
questions.boundary: The depreciation worksheet covers a bounded ordinary first-year method; it does not decide immediate-deduction eligibility.
questions.fact: An employee can deduct the work-related share of an item costing $300 or less straight away, unless it is part of a set costing more than $300; a dearer item is depreciated over its effective life. A small business with aggregated turnover under $10 million can write off each eligible asset costing less than $20,000.

questions.question: Which work clothing, uniforms and laundry expenses can I claim?
questions.answer: Work clothing claims depend on the type of clothing and its connection to your work. Wearing ordinary clothes at work does not establish a claim.
steps: Separate protective clothing, qualifying uniforms, occupation-specific clothing and ordinary items.
Retain purchases and a supportable laundry calculation, with any reimbursement recorded.
questions.boundary: Check the ATO category and evidence requirements before adding an amount to the return.
questions.fact: You can claim clothing that is protective, a compulsory uniform, a registered non-compulsory uniform, or occupation-specific and not conventional. Laundry can be worked out at $1 a load of work clothing only, or 50 cents a load if mixed, and a laundry claim of $150 or less needs no written evidence.

questions.question: Can I claim course fees, professional memberships and self-education expenses?
questions.answer: Check how the course or membership relates to your current income-earning activities.
steps: Keep invoices, course details, the work connection and any employer reimbursement.
Split private components and costs of gaining a new occupation from costs relevant to current work for review.
questions.boundary: A professional label or employer recommendation alone does not settle the tax treatment.
questions.fact: Self-education is deductible when it maintains or improves the specific skills or knowledge you need for your current employment, or is likely to increase your income from it.

questions.question: What can I claim if I have lost the receipt?
questions.answer: Try to replace missing evidence before deciding whether a claim can be supported.
steps: Request duplicate invoices or download supplier records and match them to payment evidence.
Write down the expense, work purpose, missing record and the ATO evidence rule you relied on.
questions.boundary: A bank statement or a general receipt exception does not automatically support every claim.
questions.fact: If your total work-related expense claim is $300 or less, you can claim it without written evidence, but you must be able to show how you worked it out. Keep any written evidence for 5 years from the date you lodge your return.

questions.question: Does my business qualify for the instant asset write-off this financial year?
questions.answer: Test eligibility against the rules enacted for the asset’s relevant year and circumstances.
steps: Record aggregated turnover, asset cost, acquisition and first use dates, and business use share.
Check the current ATO small business depreciation rules, including exclusions and any applicable election.
questions.boundary: The ordinary depreciation worksheet does not determine instant asset write-off eligibility.
questions.fact: Yes, if your aggregated turnover is under $10 million and you use the simplified depreciation rules. You can deduct the full cost of each eligible asset costing less than $20,000 that is first used or installed ready for use in the year. The $20,000 limit applied in 2025-26 and is permanent from 1 July 2026.

questions.question: Do I need an ABN for freelance or contracting work?
questions.answer: ABN entitlement depends on carrying on or starting an enterprise. An invoice or a client’s request alone does not establish it.
steps: Record the work arrangement, independence, activity and evidence that the enterprise has started.
Read the ABR entitlement guidance before applying.
questions.boundary: An ABN does not decide whether a worker is an employee for tax, super or workplace law.
questions.fact: You’re entitled to an ABN if you’re carrying on or starting an enterprise in Australia. You’re not entitled to one for work you do as an employee, even if you or your employer calls it contracting.

questions.question: How do I apply for an ABN, and what information do I need?
questions.answer: Apply through the official ABR route after checking entitlement.
steps: Gather the entity structure, business activity, start date and contact information required by the ABR.
Enter identity information directly into the official application and save its confirmation.
questions.boundary: This site neither applies for an ABN nor handles identity documents.
questions.fact: Apply online through the ABR. Details such as your TFN help the ABR identify you and process the application faster; if it needs to check details, it aims to review the application within 20 business days.

questions.question: Is my activity a hobby or a business for tax purposes?
questions.answer: Assess the pattern of activity, commercial purpose and how the activity is organised.
steps: Document your intention, pricing, repetition, scale, records and plan to make a profit.
Keep the conclusion and supporting facts, and reassess when the activity changes.
questions.boundary: There is no single revenue figure in this guide that classifies every activity.
questions.fact: Generally, a business involves continuous and repeated activities done to make a profit. The ATO asks whether you intend to and have a prospect of making a profit, whether the scale is enough to make one, and whether the activities are repeated and continuous; a hobby you don’t seek to profit from is not a business.

questions.question: Should I operate as a sole trader or a company?
questions.answer: Compare liability, ownership, administration, tax and how profits will reach the owners.
steps: Prepare the same forecast under each structure, including compliance costs and money taken out.
Discuss asset protection, existing contracts and restructuring costs with the relevant advisers before choosing.
questions.boundary: A lower company tax rate alone does not establish a lower total cost or a suitable structure.
questions.fact: A sole trader reports business income as their own and is personally liable for the business’s debts. A company is a separate legal entity with higher set-up and running costs and an annual ASIC review; it pays tax at 25% or 30%, and it pays directors wages or fees rather than drawings.

questions.question: How much should I set aside for income tax as a sole trader?
questions.answer: Reserve cash against an estimate of your annual personal tax position and instalments already paid.
steps: Forecast business profit alongside salary and other personal income, deductions and credits.
Place expected instalments and the remaining tax payment into the cash forecast on their due dates.
questions.boundary: A fixed percentage of sales can miss deductions, other income and tax already paid.
questions.fact: The ATO automatically enters an individual, including a sole trader, into PAYG instalments when their latest return shows instalment income of $4,000 or more, tax payable of $1,000 or more and estimated tax of $500 or more. You can also enter voluntarily.

questions.question: Do I need a separate business bank account?
questions.answer: A separate account makes business transactions easier to trace. The requirements also depend on the entity.
steps: Record which accounts hold business money and reconcile each to its statement.
For a company or trust, keep entity funds and private funds clearly identified and correctly recorded.
questions.boundary: Check the account requirements for your structure before opening or changing banking arrangements.
questions.fact: A sole trader doesn’t have to have a business bank account, although it’s a good idea. A partnership, company or trust must have a separate bank account for tax purposes.

questions.question: How do I pay myself and record drawings as a sole trader?
questions.answer: Sole-trader drawings transfer the owner’s money out of the business; they are recorded separately from operating expenses.
steps: Record the transfer against drawings or the owner’s equity account in your agreed chart.
Keep drawings visible in the cash forecast so the business can meet upcoming obligations.
questions.boundary: A sole trader’s drawings do not set the amount of taxable business profit.
questions.fact: What you draw doesn’t change what a sole trader reports: all your business income goes in your individual tax return, whatever amounts you transfer to your personal account.

questions.question: Do the personal services income rules apply to my contracting income?
questions.answer: Review whether the income is mainly a reward for personal effort or skill, then work through the applicable PSI tests.
steps: Keep contracts, invoices, working arrangements and evidence for any test relied on.
Record the income streams separately and review personal-services-business conditions with your adviser.
questions.boundary: An ABN or company structure does not by itself switch off the PSI rules.
questions.fact: For income that is mainly a reward for your personal effort or skill, the PSI rules apply when 80% or more of it comes from one client and its associates, unless you pass the results test or hold a personal services business determination.

questions.question: How do I report income from a side hustle, delivery work or online sales?
questions.answer: Reconcile gross platform activity to payouts before deciding how to report it.
steps: Export sales, fees, refunds and activity records for the income year.
Document whether the activity is business, employment or another income category and check GST separately.
questions.boundary: Net bank deposits can omit fees and gross receipts that need separate reporting.
questions.fact: Income from providing services or assets for a fee through a sharing economy platform, such as ride-sourcing, renting out a room or sharing assets, is taxable, and GST can apply. Platform operators report these transactions to the ATO.

questions.question: Can I offset a business loss against my salary or other income?
questions.answer: A business loss needs a separate review before it can reduce other income.
steps: Keep the loss calculation, activity history and records relevant to the non-commercial loss tests.
Record whether an exception, test or discretion applies, or whether the loss must be deferred.
questions.boundary: A loss in the accounts does not automatically offset salary in the tax return.
questions.fact: Only if you meet the non-commercial loss rules: your income for the income requirement must be under $250,000 and you must pass one of 4 tests, such as earning at least $20,000 of assessable income from the business. Otherwise the loss is deferred.

questions.question: How do I add GST to a price or extract GST from an inclusive amount?
questions.answer: The calculation applies to a wholly taxable sale; classify GST-free, input-taxed and mixed sales first.
steps: Choose whether your amount already includes GST, then calculate the components.
Keep the source invoice and confirm that the whole amount is subject to GST.
questions.boundary: The calculator does not classify GST-free, input-taxed or mixed supplies.
questions.fact: GST is 10% of the GST-exclusive price. To find the GST included in a GST-inclusive price, divide it by 11: $110 includes $10 of GST.

questions.question: When must my business register for GST?
questions.answer: Check current and projected GST turnover and any compulsory-registration rule for your activity.
steps: Build a monthly turnover schedule and review what counts towards GST turnover.
Use the ATO registration guidance to determine the trigger and registration date.
questions.boundary: Taxi and ride-sourcing rules and other exceptions mean a general turnover threshold is not enough.
questions.fact: Register within 21 days once your GST turnover reaches $75,000 ($150,000 for a non-profit). Taxi and ride-sourcing drivers must register whatever their turnover.

questions.question: What is the difference between GST-free and input-taxed sales?
questions.answer: Classify each sale before coding it, because the category decides whether GST credits on related purchases can be claimed.
steps: Classify each income stream using the ATO guidance and retain the basis for the classification.
Review purchase credits and any apportionment separately for input-taxed activities.
questions.boundary: Do not give both categories the same purchase-credit treatment just because no GST appears on the sale.
questions.fact: Neither includes GST in the price. You can claim GST credits for purchases you use to make GST-free sales, but not for purchases that relate to input-taxed sales, such as financial supplies and selling or renting out residential premises.

questions.question: Do I charge GST when selling to overseas customers?
questions.answer: An overseas customer does not automatically make a sale GST-free.
steps: Record what you sold, where it is supplied or used, customer circumstances and any export evidence.
Check the relevant goods or services rule before choosing the GST code.
questions.boundary: Export conditions and evidence requirements differ between goods and services.
questions.fact: Exported goods are GST-free if they are exported within 60 days of the earlier of receiving any payment or issuing an invoice for them. Some other supplies for consumption outside Australia, such as certain services, can also be GST-free.

questions.question: What information must appear on a valid tax invoice?
questions.answer: Use an invoice checklist matched to the sale and the ATO’s tax invoice requirements.
steps: Check supplier identity and ABN, date, description, price and how the GST amount is shown.
Check any buyer-identification requirement and clearly separate taxable and non-taxable items.
questions.boundary: Requirements depend on the amount and nature of the sale; a heading alone does not make an invoice valid.
questions.fact: If a customer asks, you must issue a tax invoice within 28 days for any sale over $82.50 including GST. It must show that it is a tax invoice, your identity and ABN, the date, what was sold with quantity and price, the GST amount and how much of each sale is taxable. Sales of $1,000 or more must also show the buyer’s identity or ABN.

questions.question: How do I prepare a BAS from my accounting records?
questions.answer: Reconcile source records to each BAS label before approval.
steps: Check reporting period and GST basis, reconcile tax-coded transactions and investigate exceptions.
Reconcile PAYG and other labels, retain the workpaper and obtain approval before lodgement.
questions.boundary: The linked readiness gate checks a prepared pack. It does not prepare the BAS, decide tax treatment or authorise lodgement.
questions.example: For a fictional quarter, reconciled GST on sales at label 1A is $3,000 and eligible GST credits at label 1B are $1,800. The GST component payable is $1,200. Keep the sales and purchase reconciliations with the BAS workpaper, then reconcile other applicable BAS obligations separately. This example assumes the supplied GST amounts are already classified correctly.
questions.fact: If your GST turnover is under $10 million, you generally report GST using Simpler BAS: total sales at G1, GST on sales at 1A and GST on purchases at 1B.

questions.question: When is my BAS due, and when must I pay it?
questions.answer: Use the period and due date shown for your BAS account.
steps: Record both lodgement and payment deadlines and any approved concession.
Put the cash payment in the forecast and assign someone to retain the receipt.
questions.boundary: General quarterly dates can differ from the dates that apply to your account.
questions.fact: Quarterly BAS is due on 28 October, 28 February, 28 April and 28 July. Monthly BAS is due on the 21st day of the following month. Payment is due by the same date.

questions.question: Should I account for GST on a cash or accrual basis?
questions.answer: Compare the timing of receipts and payments under the methods your business is allowed to use.
steps: Check eligibility and the method currently recorded with the ATO.
Model the effect on unpaid invoices and bills before changing method, and document transition adjustments.
questions.boundary: Changing a report setting in Xero does not by itself change the ATO accounting method.
questions.fact: A business with aggregated turnover under $10 million can choose either the cash or the accrual basis for GST.

questions.question: Why does my BAS GST figure differ from the GST balance in Xero?
questions.answer: Bridge the BAS calculation to the GST control account at the same date and on the same basis.
steps: Separate opening balances, payments to the ATO, cash-basis timing and journals.
List each reconciling item and clear unexplained differences before signing off.
questions.boundary: A control account balance is not automatically the GST payable for one BAS period. The linked gate tests supplied tie-outs; it does not investigate reconciling items.
questions.fact: On the cash basis, you account for GST on the BAS covering the period in which you receive or make payment for your sales and purchases.

questions.question: How do I correct a mistake in a BAS I have already lodged?
questions.answer: Work out whether the error can be corrected on a later BAS or requires a revision.
steps: Record the original period, error type, amount, discovery date and supporting transactions.
Apply the ATO’s correction conditions and retain the approved amendment or later-period adjustment.
questions.boundary: Do not choose a later-period correction without checking the period of review and the 4-year credit time limit.
questions.fact: You can generally correct a GST error on a later BAS lodged within the period of review for the period of the error, but not to claim GST credits after the 4-year time limit, and not more than once. Revising the earlier BAS instead can attract penalties or general interest charge.

questions.question: How much super must I pay, and which earnings count towards it?
questions.answer: Identify the applicable super regime and eligible earnings for the pay date before calculating a contribution.
steps: From July 2026, use the ATO Payday Super guidance and map each pay component to the relevant earnings definition.
Check worker eligibility, limits and payroll settings; retain the calculation and contribution evidence.
questions.boundary: The old quarterly SG worksheet does not establish current Payday Super entitlement.
questions.fact: The super guarantee rate is 12%, as it has been since 1 July 2025. From 1 July 2026 it is worked out on qualifying earnings, up to a maximum contribution base of $270,830 for 2026-27.

questions.question: By what date must a super contribution reach the employee’s fund?
questions.answer: Test receipt at the employee’s fund against the applicable deadline.
steps: Record payday, pathway, amount, remittance date and confirmed fund receipt date.
Use the existing timing example to distinguish timely remittance from evidence of timely receipt.
questions.boundary: The timing tool needs the contribution amount supplied and the correct pathway selected.
questions.fact: Since 1 July 2026, the fund must receive the contribution within 7 business days after payday, or within 20 business days for the first contribution for a new employee or to a new fund.

questions.question: What should I do if a super payment is late, rejected or missing?
questions.answer: Investigate the payment trail and apply the current late-payment process.
steps: Reconcile payroll, clearing house status, rejections and fund receipt for each affected employee.
Resolve the cause, record any replacement payment and review the ATO’s reporting and charge requirements.
questions.boundary: Sending a replacement does not automatically remove a late-payment consequence.
questions.fact: Since 1 July 2026, super that is unpaid, late, short or paid to the wrong fund makes you liable to the super guarantee charge, which the ATO assesses. The charge includes notional earnings and may include an administrative uplift of up to 60%; paying the fund what you owe as soon as possible, even in part, reduces it.

questions.question: Do I have to pay super for a contractor who invoices through an ABN?
questions.answer: Review the actual contract and working arrangement against the ATO’s super eligibility guidance.
steps: Record who performs the work, how they are paid and whether the contract is for their labour.
Retain the eligibility conclusion separately from the supplier’s ABN and invoice.
questions.boundary: An ABN is not proof that super is unnecessary.
questions.fact: If you pay a contractor under a contract that is mainly for their labour, meaning more than half its dollar value, they are an employee for super guarantee purposes and you may need to pay super for them. An ABN makes no difference.

questions.question: How much PAYG tax should I withhold from an employee’s pay?
questions.answer: Use the ATO withholding calculation for the payment type and pay period.
steps: Check the declaration, residency, tax-free threshold choice, study loan information and any variation.
Apply the current schedule or calculator and reconcile payroll totals to the withholding liability.
questions.boundary: A resident annual income tax worksheet is not a payroll withholding calculator.
questions.fact: Use the ATO tax withheld calculator or tax tables for the pay period, whether weekly, fortnightly or monthly. The employee’s TFN declaration or withholding declaration tells you whether to withhold extra for a study or training support loan.

questions.question: How do I finalise Single Touch Payroll at year-end?
questions.answer: Reconcile payroll to the ledger and ATO reporting before making the STP finalisation declaration.
steps: Check year-to-date wages, withholding, super and adjustments by employee.
Resolve discrepancies, confirm the applicable deadline and retain the finalisation evidence.
questions.boundary: An ordinary payroll submission and a finalisation declaration are different steps.
questions.fact: Make the STP finalisation declaration by 14 July each year.

questions.question: How do I calculate an employee’s final pay, including unused leave?
questions.answer: Build final pay from the employee’s entitlements and the circumstances of departure.
steps: Gather the award or agreement, termination date, unpaid hours, leave balances and notice details.
Check leave loading, redundancy and long service leave where applicable, then apply the relevant tax treatment.
questions.boundary: The generic staff cost calculator cannot determine final pay entitlements.
questions.fact: Final pay is the wages owing, including penalty rates and allowances, plus any unused annual leave with loading if it would have been paid during employment; it can also include accrued or pro rata long service leave. Sick and carer’s leave isn’t paid out, and most awards require final pay within 7 days after the last day of employment.

questions.question: When does my business become liable for payroll tax in NSW?
questions.answer: Review Australian taxable wages, NSW connection, grouping and the applicable threshold.
steps: Prepare a wages reconciliation that includes the categories Revenue NSW requires.
Check the monthly registration trigger and annual reconciliation requirements for the relevant year.
questions.boundary: Book payroll expense alone can omit taxable benefits, super or grouped wages.
questions.fact: For 2026-27, NSW payroll tax applies to taxable wages above $1,200,000 a year, at a rate of 5.45%.

questions.question: Do contractor payments count towards NSW payroll tax?
questions.answer: Contractor payments need a separate payroll tax review under the NSW relevant-contract rules.
steps: Keep the contract, services, days worked and evidence for any exclusion claimed.
Reconcile reviewed contractor amounts to the payroll tax workpaper.
questions.boundary: An invoice, ABN or GST registration alone does not establish an exclusion.
questions.fact: Payments to a contractor who provides the services of a worker under a relevant contract are liable for NSW payroll tax unless an exemption applies, such as for some services provided for 90 days or less in a financial year, or services the contractor provides to the public.

questions.question: What does an employee cost after super, leave, insurance and other on-costs?
questions.answer: Add annual wages, super and the other costs you expect to pay, then consider productive capacity separately.
steps: Enter the annual super amount and other costs such as insurance, payroll tax, recruitment and equipment.
Allow for paid leave when estimating productive hours, and add relief staff costs only where expected.
questions.boundary: Do not add ordinary paid leave again if it is already included in the annual salary.
questions.fact: Start with wages plus the 12% super guarantee, then add leave, workers compensation, any payroll tax and other on-costs.

questions.question: Why does my Xero bank balance differ from my bank statement?
questions.answer: Reconcile the bank statement and Xero at the same date before posting a correction.
steps: Compare statement lines with ledger transactions, outstanding payments and deposits.
Investigate missing feeds, duplicates, opening balances and items dated outside the period.
questions.boundary: Do not post a balancing journal while the cause remains unknown.

questions.question: How do I identify and fix duplicate bank transactions in Xero?
questions.answer: Identify whether the duplicate is a statement line, an accounting transaction or both.
steps: Match date, amount, bank reference and source document; distinguish repeated genuine payments.
Use the appropriate Xero correction after review, then rerun the bank reconciliation.
questions.boundary: Removing the wrong item can remove a real transaction; retain the correction trail.

questions.question: How do I correct a customer payment matched to the wrong invoice?
questions.answer: Trace the payment and both customer invoices before changing the match.
steps: Save the original allocation details and check whether the invoice or period is locked.
Correct the allocation through Xero’s supported workflow and recheck both customer balances and the bank reconciliation.
questions.boundary: A different bank receipt should not be created merely to fix an allocation.

questions.question: How do I record a personal purchase paid from the business account?
questions.answer: Code the private payment according to the entity and the person’s relationship to it.
steps: Keep the receipt, purpose and repayment evidence, and separate any business portion.
For a sole trader, review drawings; for a company, review the director or shareholder account and tax consequences.
questions.boundary: A company payment cannot automatically be treated as sole-trader drawings.

questions.question: Which business records should I keep, and for how long?
questions.answer: Keep records that let someone trace transactions, calculations and decisions for the required retention period.
steps: Create a register covering tax, payroll, assets, loans, contracts and entity records.
Assign retention dates using the relevant ATO and other legal requirements, including longer periods for continuing assets or disputes.
questions.boundary: Do not apply one blanket retention date to every document.
questions.fact: Keep most business records for 5 years. Keep records for depreciating assets and CGT assets until 5 years after you dispose of the asset.

questions.question: How should I organise my chart of accounts?
questions.answer: Use a chart of accounts that supports reporting and reconciliations at a manageable level of detail.
steps: Separate assets, liabilities, equity, revenue and expenses; keep control accounts identifiable.
Use consistent account mappings and tracking categories for the dimensions you need to report.
questions.boundary: Do not create a new account for every customer or supplier when the subledger already tracks them.

questions.question: How do I split a loan repayment between principal and interest?
questions.answer: Split each repayment using the loan statement and the agreement. Interest is a finance cost; principal reduces the loan balance.
steps: Reconcile opening principal, advances, principal repayments and closing principal.
Use the loan calculator to sense-check a fixed-rate monthly schedule, then compare with the lender’s statement.
questions.boundary: Fees, daily interest, variable rates and balloons need the actual lender schedule.

questions.question: Should a purchase be recorded as an asset or an expense?
questions.answer: Apply your accounting policy to the nature, use and expected benefit of the purchase, then assess tax separately.
steps: Record what was acquired, cost, useful life and when it became available for use.
If capitalised, update the asset register and depreciation; document any tax difference.
questions.boundary: An accounting asset policy and an immediate tax deduction rule can give different treatments.

questions.question: Why do my aged receivables or payables differ from the general ledger?
questions.answer: Compare the aged report and ledger on the same date with the same filters.
steps: Trace journals to control accounts, prepayments, credits, foreign-currency adjustments and excluded contacts.
Prepare a bridge to the ledger and resolve unexplained items before closing.
questions.boundary: A matching total alone does not establish that individual balances are collectible or payable.
questions.keywords: debtors creditors accounts receivable accounts payable

questions.question: What should I reconcile and check before closing the month or financial year?
questions.answer: Close from reconciled balances and documented review decisions.
steps: Reconcile bank, receivables, payables, GST, payroll, super, loans, fixed assets and key accruals.
Review cut-off, unusual journals and variances, then retain the pack and approval before locking the period.
questions.boundary: The existing close pack supports review; it does not automatically approve journals or finalise accounts.
questions.example: At 30 September 2026, a fictional bank statement shows $12,000 and the ledger bank account shows $11,700. A $300 customer receipt is on the statement but missing from the ledger. After confirming the invoice and posting the missing receipt, both bank balances are $12,000. The aged receivables report still shows $9,500 against a $10,000 control account. Record that separate $500 exception, its owner and the evidence needed to resolve it before completing the close.

questions.question: How do I build a 13-week cash flow forecast?
questions.answer: Forecast cash by the week it is expected to move through the bank.
steps: Start with the reconciled bank balance and schedule receipts, suppliers, wages, tax, debt and drawings across 13 weeks.
Use the browser forecast for a short scenario, or the existing workbook for a detailed worked example.
questions.boundary: Weekly closing balances can hide a shortage within the week; review daily timing where cash is tight.
questions.example: Start a fictional forecast on 28 September 2026 with $200 opening cash and a $100 buffer. Enter $1,000 receipts and $300 payments in week 1, and zero in every later week. Closing cash is $900. Delay the full $1,000 receipt by two weeks: cash closes at minus $100 in weeks 1 and 2, then returns to $900 in week 3. The lowest balance is minus $100, so the funding gap to the buffer is $200. The eventual closing balance is unchanged.

questions.question: Why is my business profitable but short of cash?
questions.answer: Profit and cash diverge because income and expenses can be recognised at different times from receipts and payments.
steps: Bridge profit to cash using receivables, payables, inventory, tax, capital spending, debt and drawings.
Use the fictional Newcastle example to inspect a profitable business with a temporary cash shortage.
questions.boundary: Loan proceeds and principal repayments affect cash without being ordinary trading revenue and expense.

questions.question: How much cash should I reserve for BAS, payroll and super payments?
questions.answer: Schedule the actual expected liabilities and payment dates, then choose a buffer.
steps: Reconcile GST, withholding and super liabilities to their supporting workpapers.
Enter their payment weeks in the cash forecast, including other committed cash costs.
questions.boundary: The forecast reserves supplied amounts; it does not calculate statutory liabilities from sales.

questions.question: What happens to my cash balance if a major customer pays 30 or 60 days late?
questions.answer: Move the expected receipt to its revised date and compare the lowest cash balance.
steps: Use the weekly forecast’s delayed-receipt controls and retain both scenarios.
For an exact 30- or 60-day delay, use the existing dated workbook and record any receipt outside its horizon.
questions.boundary: The browser scenario accepts whole weeks, so it is not an exact day-based simulation.

questions.question: Can my business afford another employee?
questions.answer: Compare the extra cash costs of hiring with conservative additional receipts and available cash.
steps: Calculate annual staff cost, then phase wages, super, setup costs and training into the forecast.
Test slower sales, a delayed start and a minimum cash buffer before committing.
questions.boundary: Annual profitability does not establish that each payroll payment will be affordable.

questions.question: What would buying equipment outright versus financing it do to my cash flow?
questions.answer: Compare the timing and total payments of outright purchase and finance.
steps: Put the purchase price into the relevant cash week for the outright option.
For finance, schedule deposit, fees, repayments and any balloon; compare the cash minimum and total cost.
questions.boundary: The loan calculator assumes fixed monthly payments with no fees or balloon. Tax and ownership effects require separate review.

questions.question: How much working capital or overdraft capacity will I need next quarter?
questions.answer: Find the lowest forecast balance and compare it with the cash buffer you need.
steps: Include current bank cash, committed payments, realistic receipts and stressed collection dates.
Use the forecast funding gap result as an initial amount to investigate, then review timing and facility terms.
questions.boundary: A calculated gap is not a credit approval or proof that borrowing is suitable.

questions.question: How can I reduce overdue customer balances and get paid sooner?
questions.answer: Prioritise overdue balances by amount, age, dispute and likelihood of collection.
steps: Reconcile the aged ledger, assign an owner and record the next action for each overdue account.
Review invoice accuracy, payment terms and billing timing; update receipt dates using what customers confirm.
questions.boundary: Changing a forecast date does not improve collection evidence.

questions.question: How do I plan for seasonal cash shortages?
questions.answer: Plan from the seasonal payment and receipt pattern, including the costs incurred before sales arrive.
steps: Compare prior periods with current orders, staffing and supplier commitments.
Stress-test the low season and put any agreed funding or cost changes into the forecast.
questions.boundary: A straight average month can conceal the quarter’s lowest cash balance.

questions.question: How do I update my forecast each month using actual results?
questions.answer: Replace completed periods with reconciled actuals and explain the difference before rolling the forecast forward.
steps: Save the previous forecast, match actual receipts and payments, and classify timing versus permanent changes.
Refresh remaining assumptions and extend the horizon with a dated version and owner.
questions.boundary: Do not overwrite the old forecast if you still need it to explain accuracy and decisions.

questions.question: How much must I sell each month to break even?
questions.answer: Break-even sales cover fixed costs after variable costs. For one product, divide fixed costs by contribution per unit.
steps: Use the same period for fixed costs and the expected selling price and variable cost per unit.
Round required units up and compare them with practical sales capacity.
questions.boundary: The calculator assumes one product or a stable representative mix; it excludes tax and financing cash timing.

questions.question: What is the difference between gross margin and markup?
questions.answer: Gross margin divides gross profit by revenue. Markup divides gross profit by cost.
steps: Use sales and the directly related cost for the same goods or period.
Compare both percentages with the calculator and keep GST treatment consistent.
questions.boundary: A zero denominator has no meaningful percentage; the calculator leaves that percentage undefined.

questions.question: What hourly rate should I charge to cover costs and earn a target profit?
questions.answer: Divide annual costs plus target profit by realistic billable hours.
steps: Include the owner’s pay target in costs if it must be covered before the stated profit.
Allow for leave, administration, marketing and unpaid time when estimating billable hours.
questions.boundary: The calculated rate is a cost recovery target before GST; customers’ willingness to pay needs separate evidence.

questions.question: Which customers, jobs or service lines are making money?
questions.answer: Build contribution by customer, job or service line from consistent revenue and direct cost assignments.
steps: Allocate labour using recorded hours and identify material costs, discounts, rework and write-offs.
Keep shared overhead allocation visible and compare results before and after that allocation.
questions.boundary: An allocation method can change apparent profitability without changing total business profit.

questions.question: Why are my actual results different from my budget?
questions.answer: Compare actual and budget figures for the same period and accounting basis, then explain the drivers.
steps: Calculate the amount and percentage difference for income or costs.
Split the difference into price, volume, mix, timing, coding and one-off items, then quantify each supported explanation.
questions.boundary: The variance calculator measures the difference; it cannot infer its cause from two numbers.

questions.question: Which financial reports should a small business owner review each month?
questions.answer: Review profit, financial position and cash together, with the balances that explain them.
steps: Prepare the P&L against budget, balance sheet, cash forecast, aged debtors and creditors, and key obligation reconciliations.
Record exceptions, decisions, owners and dates for the next review.
questions.boundary: Choose detail that changes a decision; a larger dashboard does not necessarily improve the review.

questions.question: How do my business expenses compare with ATO small business benchmarks?
questions.answer: Choose the ATO industry and turnover range that match your business and reporting period.
steps: Map ledger accounts to the benchmark definitions and retain the mapping.
Compare ratios with the relevant dataset and investigate differences in business model, year or coding.
questions.boundary: The linked benchmark tool uses specified historical datasets; a difference is not proof of an error or non-compliance.

questions.question: How do I value and report work in progress and unbilled work?
questions.answer: Separate the accounting basis for recognising revenue from the amount billed.
steps: Reconcile contract value, costs incurred, estimates to complete, billings and unbilled amounts.
For a suitable construction contract, use the WIP schedule and review estimate changes and profit fade.
questions.boundary: The existing tool covers construction cost-to-cost schedules; it does not classify every service contract.

questions.question: Why has my gross margin fallen even though sales have increased?
questions.answer: Higher sales can coincide with a lower margin when prices, product mix or costs change.
steps: Compare revenue and direct costs by job or product; check discounts, labour efficiency, rework and cut-off.
Use the margin and variance calculators, and review cost-to-complete estimates for construction work.
questions.boundary: A total sales comparison alone cannot identify which driver reduced margin.

questions.question: How do I turn Xero data into a useful Excel or Power BI management dashboard?
questions.answer: Start with reconciled exports and a small set of decisions the report needs to support.
steps: Define account mappings, periods and measures, then tie totals to Xero before adding charts.
Use the existing trial balance export and close pack, and document refresh and review steps.
questions.boundary: The export tool supplies data; this guide does not install a Power BI connector or grant Xero access.

questions.question: Does my company qualify for the lower company tax rate?
questions.answer: Test the company’s income and aggregated turnover conditions for the relevant year.
steps: Reconcile taxable income, passive income categories and connected entity information.
Use the existing company tax example only after the inputs and applicable conditions have been established.
questions.boundary: The example does not determine eligibility merely from accounting profit.
questions.fact: The 25% rate applies to a base rate entity: a company with aggregated turnover under $50 million and no more than 80% of its assessable income from base rate entity passive income. Other companies pay 30%.

questions.question: How should I record money paid to a director as wages, dividends or a loan?
questions.answer: Record a director payment according to its legal basis and supporting documents.
steps: Gather payroll records, dividend documents or loan terms and trace each payment.
Review withholding, super, franking and Division 7A consequences before posting or reclassifying it.
questions.boundary: Changing the ledger label does not change the underlying transaction.
questions.fact: Wages and director’s fees are assessable income to you, and the company must withhold PAYG from them. A loan to a shareholder or their associate can be treated as a dividend under Division 7A unless it is repaid, or put under a complying written agreement, before the company’s lodgment day.

questions.question: Does taking money out of my company create a Division 7A problem?
questions.answer: Review company payments, loans and debt forgiveness involving shareholders or associates under Division 7A.
steps: Reconcile the person’s account and gather agreements, dates and repayment evidence.
Use the existing review case to organise the evidence and identify unresolved legal questions.
questions.boundary: The repayment worksheet does not decide whether a loan is complying or whether a deemed dividend arises.
questions.fact: It can. A payment, loan or forgiven debt from a private company to a shareholder or their associate can be treated as a dividend under Division 7A, generally unfranked. A loan avoids this if it is fully repaid, or put under a complying written agreement, before the company’s lodgment day.

questions.question: How do I calculate the minimum yearly repayment on a complying Division 7A loan?
questions.answer: Use the minimum yearly repayment calculation for an established complying loan and the correct year.
steps: Gather the relevant opening balance, benchmark rate, remaining term and qualifying repayments.
Reproduce the existing Division 7A case, then retain the inputs and compare required with actual qualifying repayments.
questions.boundary: Eligibility, amalgamation and repayment classification must already have been reviewed.
questions.fact: The minimum yearly repayment uses the benchmark interest rate (8.77% for 2026-27 and 8.37% for 2025-26 for a 30 June year end), the unpaid balance and the remaining term. The maximum term is 7 years, or 25 years for a loan fully secured by a registered mortgage over real property.

questions.question: Which payments count as repayments of a Division 7A loan?
questions.answer: Review the source, timing and surrounding arrangements for each proposed repayment.
steps: Trace the payment through bank and loan records and identify any reborrowing or circular movement.
Document the section 109R review and qualifying amount before using the minimum repayment worksheet.
questions.boundary: A credit to a director loan account is not automatically a qualifying Division 7A repayment.
questions.fact: A repayment may not count if you reborrow a similar or larger amount from the company afterwards, or use money borrowed from the company to make it. A dividend can be set off against a minimum yearly repayment only if both exist and the offset is agreed by the end of the income year, usually 30 June.

questions.question: What must a family trust document before distributing income at year-end?
questions.answer: Build the distribution file from the deed, beneficiary position, income calculation and trustee decision.
steps: Check the deed and timing requirements, prepare the relevant income and distribution schedules, and retain resolutions.
Use the existing trust example to separate arithmetic from missing documents and unresolved entitlement.
questions.boundary: The tool cannot validate a deed or cure a late or ineffective trustee decision.
questions.fact: A resolution making beneficiaries presently entitled to trust income is only effective for tax if it is made by 30 June, or earlier if the deed requires. If it isn’t effective, the trustee or other beneficiaries may be assessed instead, and a trustee may be taxed at the top rate.

questions.question: How do dividends and franking credits affect my tax return?
questions.answer: Reconcile the dividend statement to cash received, the franked or unfranked amount and franking credits.
steps: Record any foreign, trust or other adjustments and the relevant holding period evidence.
Use the ATO investment and imputation guidance to determine what appears in the return.
questions.boundary: A stated franking credit does not automatically establish entitlement to use the offset.
questions.fact: A franking credit is tax the company has already paid on the dividend. Include the dividend and franking credit in your return; the credit reduces your tax, and an eligible individual gets any excess refunded. If your franking credits for the year total $5,000 or more, you must have held the shares at risk for at least 45 days (90 for preference shares).

questions.question: Does providing a company car or paying an employee’s private expenses create FBT?
questions.answer: Identify the benefit, recipient, private use and FBT year before valuing anything.
steps: Gather vehicle records or expense invoices, employee contributions and any claimed exemption evidence.
Apply the appropriate valuation method and reconcile the resulting taxable value to the FBT workpaper.
questions.boundary: The existing worksheet grosses up supplied taxable values; it does not decide whether a benefit or exemption exists.
questions.fact: It can. FBT applies if a company car is used or available for an employee’s private use, and reimbursing or paying for an expense an employee incurs can be an expense payment fringe benefit. FBT is 47% of the grossed-up taxable value for FBT years ending 31 March.

questions.question: What information do I need to prepare an ATO payment plan proposal?
questions.answer: Prepare a proposal that shows how the debt and ongoing obligations could be paid.
steps: Reconcile the ATO debt, outstanding lodgements and available cash, and prepare a realistic payment forecast.
Use the ATO support route to discuss terms and retain any accepted arrangement.
questions.boundary: A forecast does not establish acceptance, interest relief or removal of other obligations.
questions.fact: A payment plan must clear the debt in the shortest possible fixed period, with weekly, fortnightly or monthly instalments. General interest charge keeps accruing daily, you must pay new tax debts on time, and income tax and activity statement debts need separate plans.

questions.question: Could my related businesses be grouped together for NSW payroll tax?
questions.answer: Assess the relationships between businesses against the NSW grouping rules.
steps: Prepare an ownership and control diagram, shared-employee details and financial relationships.
Document each grouping test and any exclusion application, then reconcile group wages.
questions.boundary: Separate company names or accounts do not by themselves prevent payroll tax grouping.
questions.fact: Businesses can be grouped for NSW payroll tax through related corporations, common employees, common control, tracing of interests, phoenix operators or subsuming smaller groups. Only one group member claims the tax-free threshold, against the group’s combined wages.

questions.question: Which expenses can I claim for a rental property?
questions.answer: Separate rental income, private use, borrowing costs, repairs and capital items before claiming expenses.
steps: Gather agent statements, invoices, loan interest, ownership details and rental availability records.
Apportion costs where required and reconcile the deduction schedule to the supporting documents.
questions.boundary: The treatment depends on the expense and property use; a rental label alone does not establish deductibility.
questions.fact: You can claim some rental expenses in the year you incur them, such as loan interest, council rates, repairs and maintenance, and depreciating assets costing $300 or less. Capital works, borrowing expenses and dearer depreciating assets are claimed over several years, and expenses are apportioned if you also use the property privately.

questions.question: Is work on my rental property a repair, an improvement or a depreciating asset?
questions.answer: Review what the work did to the property and when the relevant damage or condition arose.
steps: Keep invoices, scope of work, purchase condition and dates; split distinct components where supported.
Assess repair, capital works and depreciating asset treatment separately and update the relevant schedules.
questions.boundary: Cost alone does not distinguish a repair from an improvement or initial repair.
questions.fact: Repairs and maintenance are deductible in the year you incur them. Initial repairs for defects that existed when you acquired the property, improvements and replacing an entire unit of property are capital and are claimed over several years.

questions.question: How do I work out the capital gain when I sell an investment property?
questions.answer: Build the capital gains calculation from the relevant event, proceeds and adjusted cost base.
steps: Gather purchase and sale contracts, costs, ownership and occupancy history, and capital works records.
Review any exemptions, adjustments, residency and discount conditions before calculating the net result.
questions.boundary: A sale price minus purchase price calculation can omit material tax adjustments.
questions.fact: The capital gain is the capital proceeds less the cost base. An Australian resident individual who owned the property for at least 12 months can usually reduce the gain by the 50% CGT discount.

questions.question: How do capital losses and the CGT discount affect tax on shares I sell?
questions.answer: Calculate each gain or loss, apply eligible capital losses, then consider any available discount.
steps: Retain trade records, cost base adjustments, holding periods and carried-forward loss balances.
Reconcile the final calculation to the year’s CGT schedule and keep the remaining loss record.
questions.boundary: The bounded worksheet assumes the gains, losses and discount eligibility have already been established.
questions.fact: Apply capital losses first. An Australian resident individual who owned the shares for at least 12 months can then reduce the remaining gain by the 50% CGT discount.

questions.question: Do I owe tax when I sell, swap or spend cryptocurrency?
questions.answer: Review each crypto disposal and income event, including swaps and spending, rather than only withdrawals to cash.
steps: Export exchange and wallet activity, fees and Australian dollar values with dates.
Reconcile transfers between your own wallets separately from transactions that require tax review.
questions.boundary: The tax treatment depends on the activity and event; this site does not import wallets or classify transactions.
questions.fact: Often, yes. Selling crypto or swapping one crypto asset for another is a CGT event, so a gain can be taxable.

questions.question: How do I report ETF distributions and their tax adjustments?
questions.answer: Use the fund’s annual tax statement and any AMMA statement to reconcile the distribution components.
steps: Match cash, reinvestments, capital gains, foreign income and credits to the statement.
Record cost base increases or decreases and carry them into the investment register.
questions.boundary: Cash received alone can differ from the amount and components that belong in the tax return.
questions.fact: Declare ETF distributions, including amounts reinvested through a distribution reinvestment plan. Your ETF tax statement, such as an AMMA statement, shows the amounts to report and where, and non-assessable amounts mostly adjust the cost base of your units.

questions.question: What records does my accountant need for an SMSF annual return and audit?
questions.answer: Prepare the financial records and trustee evidence needed for both the return and the independent audit.
steps: Gather bank and investment records, valuations, contributions, pensions, minutes, member balances and supporting agreements.
Reconcile opening and closing balances and resolve the auditor’s record requests before finalising the return.
questions.boundary: This checklist does not perform an SMSF audit or certify compliance.
questions.fact: Trustees must appoint an approved SMSF auditor each year, at least 45 days before the SMSF annual return is due. The auditor needs a statement of financial position and an operating statement before starting, and any requested information within 14 days; the audit must be finished before the return is lodged.

questions.question: When does an investment property become liable for land tax in NSW?
questions.answer: Check ownership, land values, exemptions and any surcharge conditions for the relevant NSW land tax year.
steps: Reconcile all relevant NSW landholdings, ownership interests and valuation notices.
Use Revenue NSW’s current assessment guidance and retain the calculation and exemption evidence.
questions.boundary: Purchase price and one property’s value alone do not establish the full land tax position.
questions.fact: For the 2026 land tax year, NSW land tax applies when the combined taxable value of your land, excluding exempt land such as your home, exceeds the general threshold of $1,075,000.

questions.question: Does a Hunter Valley coal mining employer pay the Coal LSL levy?
questions.answer: The levy depends on whether each employee is an eligible employee in the black coal mining industry, then on that employee’s eligible wages for the month.
steps: List each employee’s role and check it against the Coal LSL eligible employee guidance.
Work out each eligible employee’s eligible wages for the month using the section 3B formula that applies.
questions.boundary: The calculator does not decide whether an employee is eligible; it calculates the levy on the wages you supply.
questions.fact: Yes, for eligible employees in the black coal mining industry. The employer reports and pays the levy monthly, currently 2.7% of each eligible employee’s eligible wages.
questions.keywords: Newcastle Hunter coal mining long service leave levy

questions.question: How do I choose a Newcastle accountant who can help with Xero and cash flow reporting?
questions.answer: Shortlist providers against the work you need and verify the relevant registrations.
steps: Check the TPB register for tax or BAS services, and ask who prepares and reviews the work.
Request a sample reporting pack, Xero experience, cash forecast process, responsibilities and a written scope.
questions.boundary: Location or software certification alone does not demonstrate the quality of advice or forecasting.
questions.fact: Before engaging anyone for tax work, check that they are listed on the Tax Practitioners Board register.
